But meanwhile new discoveries had turned

ing across the pond when they ran into an air
hole and all were drowned together. One body
has been recovered.

between this place and Finesville is down, and
the full details OF the accident viii not be known
until tomorrow.

The yacht Mayfiower. which had been
lying at the Brooklyn navy yard for nearly
year, sailed Saturday for Porto Rico.
having been refitted as station ship for
the governor Of the island.


The Mayflower was built for the late Og
den Goelet in 1896. 1t was considered the
most luxurious yacht afloat, and. with its
furnishings and decorations. cost about
$4,000. At the outbreak of the Spanish
American war Mrs. Goelet sold the vessel
to the government, the price paid being re-
ported as $4,000. 1t was converted into a
gunboat. and saw service in Cuban waters.
All its handsome furnishings have now
been restored.


The vessel measures 321 feet over all.
Her tonnage Is 1900. and her speed twenty
knots. The first official use which Gov.
Allen will make of the yacht will be to
bring him to this country early in July.

Washington March 16.-Secretary Hay and
Lord Pauncefote signed a protocol to-day at
the State Department extending the time al
lowed for ratification of the reciprocity treaties
between the United States and the British West
Indian islands of jamaica Turks and Caicos,
Bermuda and the British colony of Guiana. The
protocol provides that the ratifcations shall
take place possible. within twelve
months at the utmost These treaties are
pending before the Senate behind the French
reciprocity treaty, and the period allowed for
their ratification would expire, in the ordinary
course, about the end of the present month.
The extension does not mean that the State
Department has abandoned the idea of securing
action on the treaties at the present session of
Congress- but is simply precautiOn to guard
against unexpected obstacles.

Thanksgiving is generally regarded as
peculiarly American festival. The great ma
ton that dominates the continent Of North
America holds this feast day as being of
it's owr invention. But centuries before the
Pilgrim Fathers touched land at Plymouth
Rock there were thanksgiving feasts and
ceremonies in the land celebrated by the
first Americans, the once great red race
that is now dying out SO rapidly; and today
the rites are religiously observed by the
survivors, just as they were before the pale
faces came and when the tomahawk and
the swift arrow ruled the land. Wherever
tribal customs hold and the old pagan re-
ligon stirs in the blood, there the feasts are
given in praise of the Great Spirit who
made and controls the land and water and
all things that live.


The red man had no need of creed nor
book to recte his continual thanks to the
Great Spirit The strong winds and gentle
breezes hymned his ritual. The lakes. riv-
ers and brooks intoned his chants The sun,
moon and stars were the lights of his altar
and the whole of nature his psalm of praise
and thanksgiving. The one Eternal Spirit
ruled his heaven and his earth. He-no. the
Thunderer, gathered the clouds in his hands
and sfted down the vivifying rains. Ga-oh,
the West Wind controlled the tempests.
Jos-keka ruled the seasons and wakened
the day, and Ag-re-skoon inspired the war
rior to victory as he sent his great war cry
from the mountain peak to the valley.
In no tribes did the religious rites reach
a higher degree of development than among
the great federation of the Five Nations.
| The life of the IrOquois Indian was con-
tnual Thanksgiving. There were annual
feasts whereby all nature was sung and
praised. Beginning with the New Year
jubilee in February. these feastS followed in
succession each resurrection Of nature.
In April the flow of the sap was celebrated
in the maple feast and the thunderer who
had softeued the winters chain OF ice and
set the Sweet water flowing was glorifed

OCEAN CITY, Md, July IS, 1900.


What threatened to be a riot between
some Marylanders and a bunch of District
boys occurred today at Berlin, small town
about three miles from Ocean City. A
match game of base ball was scheduled,
and train was chartered to bring 300
Washingtonians over to the town to wit
ness the event The chartered train left
Ocean City at 2:05 pm, and arrived at
Berlin at 2:3O. The game was called soon
after. Much interest was displayed by the
enthused Washington people, and long be-
fore the game was started and the ball
tossed, ii was an assured fact that there
would be trouble. The pretty society girls
of The beach Were guying the Berliners ito
beat the band,' which greatly aggravated
and tormented the farmer boys.


The game started but before the first hit
was made the real battle royal was begun.
The players who represented Washington
were Frank Benjamin, Thomas A Green,

the disturbance began two of the Wash
ington boys were arrested but the consta-
bic and the police officer We're soon over

of safety The women who went along with
the boys soon changed the roofing cry to
real, bona fide tears; some tainted, others

feud over the use of the range. which has
long existed between cattle men and sheep
men. reached a climax this week, when

Greenport Long Island. Dec. 9-The schooner

is pounding hard on the rocks, and as the wind
holds high and in bad direction for her it is
thought she cannot be saved. Her crew was
taken off to-day by the life savers from the
Rocky Point station.


The Rosina On December 1 passed from her
builders. firm at Lynn. Mass. to her owner

feet long Mr.. Melpass had sent crew around
from Philadelphia to take the schooner to that
city.


The departure from Lynn was made on De-
cember 2. She had bad weather from the start
and when near Martha's Vineyard ran into
rough seas and high winds. Her small boats
were both carried away by waves. She was also
slightly damaged She put into Woods Hole.
where two new boats were obtained and what
repairs appeared necessary were made.


Her intended course was through Long Island
Sound, He'll Gate New-York Bay. and thence
down the Jersey Coast to Atlantic City, where
she was to await orders. She left Woods Hole
yesterday afternoon and made good progress
until about o'clock this morning, when the
wind shifted and began to blow from the north-
west. While standing in and facing high wind
her steering gear gave way. and, despite the ef-
she drifted toward the rocks Her anchors
would not hold, and she was soon in difficulty.
Distress signals were given and seen by the
Rocky Point crew.


The schooner was too far out for the gun, so
the surfboat was manned at o'clock. and after
an hours hard work the life savers were along
side the schooner. The four men on board were
transferred to the Hfeboat with much difficulty,
as the surfboat could not be brought close

in the water. line was passed from the

station and cared for.

ened people attempted to get down the

Leonard slid down a rope, followed by his

New England Passenger Association. In
cluded in the gathering were representa-
tives from the Canadian Pacific, Atchisou,
Chicago g. Northwestern, Chicago, Rock
Island & Pacific, Great Northern, Southern
trunk lines. -


The longlstanding troubles over railroad
rates was the question which. the confer
ence had been called to discuss For
months the so-called standard and differ
entail lines have been cutting rates to
the West and points on the Pacific slope.
The New England Passenger Association
has been the one to cut rates.


The cut rates are via Montreal, and are
$3.50 from Boston to Colorado common
points, $3.50 from Boston to California
common points, and $33.70 from Boston to
Pacific coast points. The contest all day
today centered on the refusal of the differ
entail lines out of Boston to abandon the
authorized schedule. Without reaching
any practical result the conference adj
journed to meet at 10 a. m. Monday next,
at the Hotel Waldorf-Astoria, New York.

try, mentioning among these Cecil Rhodes
and President Paul Kruger Of the Boer
republic.

mann spoke upon the canteen question. and
made plea in advocacy of the objects of
the Women's Christian Temperance Union.

when the meeting closed. Rev. E. w. Bliss,

According to mail advices received by
Surgeon General Sternberg the numerous
patients in the military hospitals in Ma

giving day. A tour of the various hos

comfortable. The diets were elaborated to
suit the occasion, and all those who were
ccnvalescent enough-and there were not

hospitals visited the supplementary hos

No pains were spared to make the patients

smiling faces which greeted the visitors in

very pretty appearance, each table being
neatly laid with snow white linen and
decorated with flowers. Altogether about
300 men, including patients. hospital corps

| OF Puget sound make merry in an an
! nual reunion. Having organized what
is now a fiourishing society. they
adopted the practice of meeting once

There are few ties closer than those

have separated themselves from the

own resources. Out OF these associa-

the events OF that earlier period are

part of them find that the memories

people together is as natural as 1t is

The pioneers of Puget sound did not


find their lines falling always in pleas
ant places. They came to country of
great possibilities but there were years
of discomfort and privation in store
for them before they could see their
hopes fulfilled. Homes had been left
far behind; a wide continent had been
crossed. and ait last their lot cast with
the few who had penetrated into what
was perhaps the most remote wilder
ness in all the country. THE new land
was sparsely settled, the means Of COM
munication were limited, and OF ne
cessity the newcomers were out OF
touch with the rest of the world. Iso-
lated by reason of the geographical
situation Of their new homes, even be-
yond what was then known as the
frontier. the pioneers of this section


were forced to rely upon themselves In
far greater degree than were those
who settled in that part OF the Western
country nearer to wealth, culture and
modern conveniences. They had pen
etrated into the heart of forest. and
TO hew out home and acquire the nee
essaries of life meant unremitting toll.
In a land which then produced little or
nothing they were dependent upon re-

times their wants were provided for but
meagerly. For religion, education and
social recreation they were forced to
| rely upon their own efforts and ingenu-
ity, and what there was of early
growth and advancement was due
| wholly to their own energy and unas-
sisted endeavors.


But there was always a spirit in that
pioneer life which softened what would
otherwise have been harsh conditions.
They had an Astounding faith in the
country with which they had cast their
fortunes. They knew the future would
certainly bring rewards. They labored

/ thousands OF earnest. eager. enterpris-
/ ing citizens, who make up some Of the
most progressive and substantial COM
munties in the land. The pioneers can
hook back and realize that they saw
| clearly They knew they had come
upon "a land Of promise. and they did


well In laying broad and deep the
! foundations Of the present splendid
! commonwealth.

Queenstown. Dec. 91.-The British steamer
Lake Megantc, Captain Taylor from Liverpool
December % and Queenstown December 26 for
st. John returned to Queenstown Harbor yes
terday Sunday morning, after terrible ex
perience in the gale. She left Queenstown
Wednesday carrying the Canadian mails FORTY
five saloon and second cabin passengers and
about five hundred steerage passengers, princi-
pally foreigners. with many Hebrews among
them. She had reached a point about four
hundred miles west Thursday night when she
encountered a merciless gale. Behaving splen
didly, she would have got through had not the
steering gear become damaged badly placing
her in a dangerous position. The crew worked
bravely and rugged hand gear, and the vessel
was again brought under control Unfortunate
ly the hand gear also became damaged


The deckhands had an awful time The gale
lasted twenty hours and an immense sea broke
over the vessel, smashing the BOBBY hatch and
flooding her between decks. where the steerage
passengers We're located. It also washed away
a greater portion of the fittings and did con-
siderable deck damage. Three lifeboats were
smashed. Some of the crew were seriously in
jured and one seaman killed on deck


When the storm moderated Captain Taylor
decided to return to Queenstown 1t was diff
cult work to steer the big ship, but she man
aged TO anchor here without assistance. Her
officers and men were exhausted.


To everybodys surprise, the Beaver Company
directed Captain Taylor TO take the Lake Me-
gantic to Liverpool, and she proceeded this
evening with all her passengers and mails TO be
transferred to the Lake Superior, which will
leave the Mersey Tuesday.


The company ordered a tug to accompany her
but none available here. Tugs will be sent
from Liverpool to meet her. There will be con-
siderable anxiety as to her safety in her present
disabled condition especially the weather
has again broken into high northwest gale


1t was impossible to interview any OF the Lake
Megantic's people, and the company's agents
are reticent; but IL is understood that there
were indescribabe among the passen-
gers who are said to have howled in despair for
hours, expecting that the steamer would founder
at any moment.

I do not believe that the Southern bor-
der States would have seeded from the
Union in 1861 but for the aid and COM
fort given them by the Copperheads of
the North. When one distinguished ora
tor declared that the Union army would
have to march over the dead bodies of
10000 Indiana Democrats before they
reached the South, the magnificent utter
ance electrified Tennessee with hope.


Thousands of men hesitated upon the
brink of the awful abyss. They loved
the Union and hated the Abolitionists.
The Union was theory" entwined with
beautiful and patriotic sentiments. Slay-
cry was condition" in which was in
vested the hard earnings of lifetime.
At the supreme crisis came the promise
of Northern Democrats that they would
not let us be hurt: their bitter denuncia-
tions of the Republican party. The South
made the leap.


During the war we saw Indiana regi-
ments and brigades march through the
State of Kentucky. "Tramp," Tramp"
"Tramp," they passed through Tenues-
see, Georgia ana South Carolina. We
never did learn how the poor fellows got
over those 10000 dead bodies of their
Democratic friends and neighbors. We
were fully persuaded they killed and
made corduroy road of them, because
the anti-imperialists of Indiana said they
would.


Our next hope after we got mixed up
together was that England and France
would help us for commercial reasons.
Vallandigham, Stevenson and thousand
other Copperheads like the good brethren
who held up Joshua's arms held ours up
by encouraging us to hold out a little
longer, by denouneing the war "fail-
ure" and keeping us posted as to the
movements of our enemies.


This is all ancient history, but 1, an old
Confederate, can see very readily how
the anti-imperialist league can materially
aid Aguinaldo and his erowd. Every old
soldier, North and South, understands
the force Of moral support. Our war
would not have lasted three months but
for Northern Democratic encouragement,
and believe Aguinaldo would have been
as peaceful a citizen as Gomez but for
the encouragement he has received from
the sentimental traitors of the Anti-Im-
perial League.


THOMAS H. BAKER.
United States Marshal Western District


of Tennessee.

fair.

Sad Eve went forth amid earth's thorny ways,
She bade goodbye to all the lovely flowers
She knew and cherished in her happy days.
Then, bending low, she kissed the snow-white


rose,


When, 10, its pure pale petals changed to red,
As though it blushed to hear of sins and woes
As Eve knelt weeping by the garden bed
Her falling tear-drops shone like pearly dew
Upon its petals as she sobbed farewell,
And deeper still its ruddy color grew,
AS, one by one, the burning tear-drops fell.
And ever since the blood-red roses blow
In sultry hours, and speak of joys and pain,
And lovers pause to pluck them as they grow.
While nightingales chant on their soft refrain.
Perchance at times they feel the piercing thorn,
Which ever guards the roses stem, tits said
Since that long-vanshed hour in Edens morn,
When sad Eve kissed the white rose petals red.

BLOEMFONTEIN, Monday. May 2S.-
Amid salutes and cheers and the singing
of God Save the Queen the military gov
ernor, Major General George Pretyman.
at noon formally proclaimed the annexa-
tion of the Free State under the designation
of the Orange River Colony. The ceremony
vas somewhat imposing and the scene In
the market square inspiring. An immense
concourse had gathered and the town was
gay with bunting. The balconies and win
dows surrounding the square were crowded
with ladies, among them Lady Roberts and
the Misses Roberts, the Countess Of Airlie
and Ladies Henry Bentick and Settrington.


The troops were drawn up under COM
mand of Gen. Knox and entertained the
spectators. The governor. accompanied by
Gen. KeIly-Kenny and their STATS, escorted
by the Welsh Yeomanry, was greeted with
a general salute after which. amid i'm
pressive silence and in a clear voice heard
in every part of the square, Gen. Pretyman
read Lord Roberts proclamation annex1n5
the Orange Free State, as conquered by her
najesty's forces, to the queens dom1nlons,
and proclaiming that the state shall hence
forth be known as the Orange River Colony.


Lusty cheers greeted the concluding
words of the proclamation, and these were
renewed with ever-increasing volume as
Lord Acheson unfurled the royal standard
and the bands struck up God Save the
Oueen.' all present joining in singing the
national hymn.


The ceremony concluded with cheers 1or
the queen Lord Roberts and the army, anu
a salute of twenty-one guns.

From the Manila American.


Any one who left Manila year ago, re-
turning to it today, would almost fancy
himself Rip Van Wrinkle.


Today one may well rub ones eyes at the
change effected. The streets, if dusty and
somewhat muddy, are at least clear of
garbage-the cutters are kept cleared.
Houses have been repaired and painted.
lnnumerable new stores have been opened
rigs have been much improved, though still
leaving much to be desired. Pariahs are
growing conspicuous by their absence, es-
peciaiiy canine ones, and the beggars are
gradually disappearing from the street
Sickness and disease are considerably on
the decrease, and the city generally is in a
more sanitary condition than it has ever
been since its foundation. And all these
changes and improvements have been
brought about by the bringing to bear,
upon the existing conditions, American
ideas in place of the aforetime LASER aller
notions existing under late Spanish rule
The wonderful improvements achieved so
far are an excellent omen for what another
year will bring forth. and those here then
will see how extremely beneficial to the city
generally and the welfare of it's inhabit-
ants has been the new regime.

The four Brooklyn marine engineers who took

and Assistant Engineers George c.. Carroll. Walter

The task of taking the Dolphin through the heavy
rolling open and the treacherous currents of
the Straits of Magellan was considered well nigh
impossible.

O'Brien. known Dynamite Johnny o. Brien.
who hailed from Seattle. The vessel reached her

meeting high winds and severe storm off Cape

Seattle, seventy-two days being consumed in the
entire passage.

in Which Her Young Had Burned.

There was tragedy enacted at the re-
cent Dearborn street fire where four wo-
men lost their lives witnessed by none of
the thousands that stood horror-stricken
as they saw men and women climbing to
safety along narrow lodges of the building
front. In a recess at one end of the large,
overhanging cornice was a pigeon home
The father and mother birds were driven
from their posts by the heat and smoke
but the three nestlngs persisted.


After the firemen had stopped work and
the excitement had died down, the parent
pigeons came back to seek their young
sticks of which the nest built and
their young were mere crisps. Toward
evening the mother bird began flying over
the ruins. She circied for a time and fin
ally landed on the roof of the wrecked
building. Soon she was Joined by her mate.
They seemed greatly puzzled at the change
the fire had wrought. The heat had melted
the Joints OF the galvanized iron cornice
which hung in great strips over the win
dows Of the top story. The pigeons looked
over the wrecked cornice, ducking their
heads and appearing to talk about their
loss


The father bird flew away, but the
mother remained. Finally she plucked up
courage enough to fly to the top OF the
upper story "lhuoW near ner nest Then
she sdled along to the stone ledge at the
bottom of the wrecked cornice. She
stretched her head toward her burned
home. and then. as If frightened at what
she saw. few to the roof again. Soon the
father bird Joined her. After a sorrowful
conference the mother bird again dropped
to the stone ledge. She was encouraged by
her mate, and crept along to the recess in
the corner of the cornice. Her mate fol-
lowed. and together they viewed their dead
offspring The mother bird crept timidly
into the nest of embers. She even tried
to cover her dead nestlings The father
kird seemed to tell her to come away, and
they soon flew to the roof again. Here an
other sad conference was held, and, after
comforting his mate, the father pigeon
few away.


Not so with the mother She kept her
vigil into the night, and was still at her
post above her wrecked home and dead
nestlings when the day closed on the scene
of destruction.

Now all were gone save these who lay at rest,
Love, hate. ambition, cold in each still breast;
The restless feet Of passing crowds, the stir
OF busy men no more to them than fear
OF this lone man, who hurried through the gloom,
His Blended shadow fitting over each white tomb
AS he FASTENED; haste, indeed, meet

The storm of pagan fury. pagan hate,

This fury in their blood-to crush a creed
That taught purer worship IN its seed.
Disr>rse the gathering numbers in its fold
Who held their faith treasure more than gold,
And human horrors light ocean foam;
Thus threatening downfall to the gods of Rome.
So had their fercest rage sought out the head
OF this sect, and hence had Peter fed;
Urged by their prayers, persuaded by the tears
OF all the Christians. torn 10y torturing fears

TACOMA. Jan. 31.--The big steamship
Goodwin, which went ashore in the fog
half a mile east Of Browns point at s:01
o'clock this morning. was pulled into deep
water and thereby rescued from her very
perilous position by the tugs Favorite and
Fairfield at 4.30 p. m.


The grounding of the Goodwin caused
more eommotion today In local shipping
circles than has been known since the
sinking of the Inflated Andelana In jan
uary, 1899 Loaded with 5000 tons of cot
ton, -four. etc, for Oriental ports, the
Goodwin pulled out from the Northern
Pacific docks at a m. and was going
straight to sea without stopping. The
fog was unusually heavy. so thick indeed
1t did not entirely clear away from over
the bay all day. Even the proximity OF
the shureOwas unknown until the bow of
the big freighter was pushing its way
through the gravel of the beach. The
engines we're Immediately driven full
steam astern, but without result


A ships boat was lowered and the mate.
with several seamen. dispatched across
the bay to notify Dodwell a. Co. the ships
charterers. The tugs Fairfield and Favor
lite were Immediately sent to render what
assistance they could. The ships an
chers were dropped overheard. astern. and
other measures taken to increase the pos
sibity of her sliding of the beach.


When the steamers agents. Capt Ciiff,
Lloyds surveyor, and her stevedore
Hamilton reached the scene In a launch
they found the bows of the Goodwin rest
ing on the gravelly beach as far back
as the bridge. For about eighty feet from
the shore the beach slopes of at about
twenty-five degrees. The slope ends
there, the water suddenly deepening from
twenty-four feet TO eleven fathoms The
steamer went ashore shortly after high
tide, and 1t was foreseen to be possible
that she might be worked or at nood
tide this afternoon Barges were accord
ingly secured. and the lghtering of the
cargo in the forward part of the vessel
commenced. About a hundred tons were
taken out. Negotiations were commenced
to have the collier Progress, now in port,
assist in hauling the steamer of. In the
meantime the Fairfield and Favorite were
exertng all their power to see-saw the
vessel down to where she would slide on
into deep water. This maneuver proved
successful at 4:90. thereby preventing
probable serious damage when the water
becomes fourteen feet lower at extreme
low tide tonight. The vessel sustained no
serious injury. and will sail some time
tomorrow. without docking.


Pilot Cater, who has been In the SER
vice of the Northern Pacific Steamship
Company for years. takes all the respon-
sfbIlity of the accident upon himself His
only excuse Is that he either lost his bear
inss swift current set him further in
shore than he realized. 1t was Pilot Cat
ter who was directing tha course OF the
Glenosie last April when she coiiidcd with
the City OF Kingston.


The grounding of the Goodwin again
proves the old adage that the more haste,
the less Speed Her sailing date was set
for Thursday. but the rapidity with which
she was loaded by the electric conveyors
used by McCabe & Hamilton made her
ready for sea one day earlier. Had she
even waited five hours longer. until the
fog began 10 lift. there would have been
no trouble.

ceived from Shanghai regarding the recent
murders of railway engineers by Boxers.
1t seems that a party of thirty, including
six ladies and one child, left Poatingfu in
twelve boats under military escort. After
traversing fifty miles in safety they missed
their way. The boats grounded and the
Boxers opened fire upon the unfortunate
occupants, using both rifles and wooden
cannon The engineers returned the fire eff
fectively and the party landed. One lady
and three men got separated from the main
body. They were brutally killed.

those able to bear arms outside and the
women inside and made off toward Tien-
tsin, They Travelled three and a half days,
fighting all the way. More than 1900 car
tridges were expended and ammunition was
running short.

a hundred rebels. The men behaved like
heroes carrying the women and children

ity.

disappeared and were murdered. The sur
vivors eventually met the rescue party, and,
much exhausted, they were escorted to
Tientsin.

NEW YORK, October 17-Eight people
were either burned to death or suffocated
in fire which partially destroyed the
three-story and attic frame double tene-
ment house 40 and 451a Hester street early
today.

Sarah Sass, thirty-six years old.


Samuel Sass, thirteen years.

Morris Sass, two years


Mrs. Horowitz, fortysiX years.


Rosa Lewis. fifty-two years.

Mary Murray, forty years old, was Sc
verely burned about the back and was
taken to hospital

o'clock by the janitor of the buildings. He
ran out into the hall to find it ablaze. His
SHOUTS aroused the others in the house, but
the flames had already gained fierce head
way and few of those in the building had

Family on Third Floor.

Sass. his wife and four children, his moth
er-in-law and Mrs. Horowtz. Sass took
the child nearest at hand and rushed to
the fire escape. He managed to get down
to the balcony in front of the building sec
ond floor, and supposed that his wife and
the others were following him Mrs Horo-
witZ was the only one who followed him
however. She took the child from his arms
when she saw their escape was cut off
and cried to a policeman below to catch
It, The policeman held out his arms, and
as the child fell he caught it safely and
shouted to her to drop


Sass had already hung down and dropped
to the ground. Mrs Morowitz was about
to drop when flames suddenly burst through
an awning on the first floor, with such fury
that she was driven back against the wall
and her only escape cut off. So fierce were
the flames that they burst at the same
time from the awning below from the win
dew behind her and from the floor of the
balcony under her feet that it was impos-
s!bie for the fremen to rescue her. On the
balcony. only a few feet above the ground
but hedged in all sides by flames she
was burned to death before the eyes of
the horritied crowd gathered in the street.


Mother and Son Perish.


Mrs. Sass, with little Morris, had been
unable to get further than the window when
they We're both overcome by smoke and
perished. Lena Sass ran into the hallway
ana was caught by the flames there and
died. Samuel tried to rescue Mrs Rosa
Lewis from the flames, but was unsuccess-
full and they pershed together. Their
>
arms still clasped about the aged womans
waist, though he had died while try

The front room in the attic was occu-
pied by Menle Strauss and his son Samuel
Both were suffocated before they could es-

Mary Murray and Mary Martin, scrub

Newcastle Friday. May 1S.-The British
troops entered Newcastle to-day and hoisted
the Union Jack over the Town Hall. The Beers
passed through Tuesday, disorganized mob.
There thirty families here. All the stores
and private houses had been looted but the
buildings not much damaged.


Natal is practically clear Of Beers.


Dundee Thursday, May 1.-THE British in
fantry passed through Newcastle at o'clock
A few residents were congregated at street cor
ners, wearing the national colors. After their
walk Of twenty-five miles the men appeared in
splendid style.


The Beers are endeavorng to reorganize along
the Heidelberg hills. Many rebels have been
found on the farms well supplied with ammuni-
ton and arms.


Recent visitors to Johannesburg say the Beers
are beginning to realize the seriousness OF their
to become Of them. The Boer women carry
rifles in the streets, and eager to go to the
commanders They say the British will not fire
upon them.


Muller, a former officer in the Prussian army,
refused $50 month and commission from the
Beers to succeed Colonel Schiel the captured
artillery commander.


A tremendous quantity OF looted furniture was
found stored in the Town Hall Evidently the
Beers had intended to burn It, but they were
prevented by the hurry Of the evacuation.


The three span bridge at Ingagone has been
destroyed and the station burned. The Beers
blew up the water tank and destroyed the water
works pipes, but the system can be renewed.

Eleven hundred volts of electricity yesterday
passed through the body of Chief Engineer Joseph
Farnsworth, of the East Chester Electric Light
Company. Of Mount Vernon. Notwithstanding that
under ordinary circumstances fewer volts pro-
duce death, Farnsworth will recover. Farnsworth.
who is resident Of New-Rochele. engaged
at noon in changing the plugs a switchboard
when he received the shock He clutched the plug
in his hand and unable to let go.


Two electricians employed by the company saw
Farnsworth lying the floor clutchng the plug.
His eyes protruded and his muscles stretched
to their highest tension. Fred Murmann rushed
to the switchboard and cut off the current. The
injured man was picked up unconscious with blood
flowing from his ears and nose. His head was
badly bruised from falling against the machinery
A physician was summoned. who worked over
Farnsworth until he resuscitated, after which
taken home in carriage. The mans
escape puzzled the physicians and the electricians
They declare that he must have wonderful con-
stitution and exceptionally strong heart.

Cotton continues to grow very rapidly.

Saturdays game between Georgetown and
Lafayette proved exceptionally interesting
to the followers of the local team The
wearers of the blue and gray resemble
thoroughbred horse trained for the mile
and-a-h half distance-the further they go the
better they get. The great improvement in
team work and all-around confidence of the
Georgetown boys>was quickly seen, and the
future certainly looks bright for them.


The Lafayette lads started off well and
for four innings held the lead, but they
were doing little with the bat and had easy
fielding chances, their lead being established
through lucky playing. The local collie
gians were in something of the same shape
in the matter of hitting, but their fielding
chances were hard. but well taken care of.
In the fifth Georgetown simply got into its
right stride, and from then to the finish it


was a walk-over, the final score being IL
to g.


Golden and Blewitt did the twirling for


the locals. while Plat and Johnson did the
same for the visitors. AS usual with young
pitchers, both teams were handicapped with
their wildness, but~the Lafayettes suffered


the most, as their free passes were given


when the hitting began. The fielding or


both teams can be described as brilliant.
although First Baseman Bachman had
three misplays and Shortstop Currier two.
The presence of Moran at short for the
Georgetown meant great deal to his team.


The little fellow is a ball player all over.
and his aggressiveness puts confidence in
his companions, and result a winning
combination is quickly formed. Lafayettes
team is considered quite a strong one. and
the ease with which they were defeated
augurs well for Georgetown's chances
against the clubs from the big colleges.

A dispatch from Cedar Rapids. Ia. last

5 o'clock this morning killed James F1tz-

riously and possibly fatally injured Mrs

Saturday night, about 10 o'clock, clad

Shortly before 5 o'clock this morning

Ladies Home, was awakened by crashing
glass. The next moment Mefford stood be-
fore him, stark naked, swinging neck
yoke.


Your time has comet shouted Mefford


"What time do you mean?' asked An
drews, with remarkable GOODNESS.


81 have murdered one whole family to-
night and I am going to kill you next. and
then everybody in the home" replied Mef-
ford.


Mefford swung the neck yoke and tried
to brain Andrews. The latter lodged and
grabbed the weapon. threw Mefford on the
bed and choked him until he begged for
mercy. Then Andrews agreed to give him
a bath. a suit of clothes and some break
fast which apparently satisfied him.


Rushing through the house, Andrews
locked the twelve or fourteen old ladies in

phone and then ran across the street to
the home of Joseph Drake for assistance

they started out.

yards away. AS he entered the room Mrs

swung the ak and brought it down toward
her head. Her uDlifted arm saved her
life: the arm was broken in two places, and
she sustained serious scalp wound.


Mr.. FitZsimmons. hearing her scream
dashed into the room and grappled with
the maniac Mefford shook him off and
sent the ak crashing into his skull. split
ting his head wide open. Then. dashing up
stairs. Mefford attacked Miss Kate Fitz-
simmons. inflicting a number of severe
scalp wounds.


When he came down stairs Drake had
just entered the house. Drake dropped to
his knees to shoot. but the revolver ham
mer merely clicked upon four empty cham
bers. Then Mefford was upon him and
struck him on the head with the ak. A
second and third blow followed and Drake

Andrews escaped the maniac again.


Mefford seized brakes revolver and ran
out of the house. After running several
blocks he fired one of the two bullets the
weapon contained into his left breast, just
below the heart. Running on two or three
blocks farther, he sat down on the curb
stone. Placing the revolver to the center
of his forehead, he fired again. He con-

but just as the first of the pursuing police

Paris April 29-An accident within the Expo
sition grounds caused the death of nine persons
and injured many others. A temporary bridge
broke, falling on pedestrians passing beneath.


The accident threw a pail over the happiness
of an immense throng who had profted by the
magnificent weather to visit the Exposition. To-
days probably the record attendance. Not
merely the interior of the grounds, but the pre-
cincts also We're crowded. and the concourse
particularly great along the Avenue de Suffren,
which forms the northern boundary of the
grounds. Here is situated big side show, the
Celestial Globe. A footbridge. which the
finishing touches were being put to-day, crossed
the Avenue de Suffren, connecting the side show
with the Exposition. 1t constructed of
wood, with a stucco facade and with plaster
made tower at each end.


Strangely enough, the bridge had been
demned only this morning as unsafe by the Ex-
position authorities The public therefore
not allowed to go upon this structure, and in
this way disaster more terrible than that
which occurred was averted


KILLED WITHOUT WARMING


The gay crowd passing along the avenue
and some hundred or more persons walk
ing beneath the bridge, when suddenly omi-
nous crash was heard. Before those underneath
could turn aside the structure fell with fearful
crash, burying nearly fifty. A shout of horror
rose from the spectators, mingled with the cries
of the victims For moment nothing could be
distinguished but a cloud of dust and plaster.
scene of the greatest excitement and confusion
followed. But this only for few seconds,
Almost Immediately the crowd attacked the de-
bris in effort to release those lying beneath.


The workmen within the grounds who had
witnessed the accident, the police and the Re
publican Guards together with quite number
of soldiers, joined In the rescue work The
promenaders forgot their Sunday attire and COW
cred themselves with dirt and CRIME in tearing
away the rubbish with their hands Wooden
beams and poles were hastily brought from the
half finished buildings near by and were used
levers to raise the fallen mass.


The victims first recovered were mostly only
the injured. the dead being found later beneath
the centre of the structure. Messengers were
dispatched to bring ffremen and sappers, with
their equipments and the first body vas found
after a quarter of an hours frantic labor. 1t
that of little girl about years old.
whose head was crushed. Victim after victim
brought to light. until a of nine mutt
lated corpses had been placed upon the side
walk. and a score of other persons, some badly
and others less seriously injured, had been car
ried in ambulances or driven to the hospitals.
PARENTS KILLED, CHILDREN ESCAPE.


family composed of father, mother and two
girls narrowly escaped destruction The pRFerItg,.
who happened TO be a little ahea :. had gone un-
der the bridge. the children following just at
the moment of the collapse. The parents were
killed, but the children sprang back and
capped with a few scratches A cyclist had his
wheel smashed. but he escaped unhurt.


The weighty plaster towers seem to have been
responsible for the fall of the structure. Com
missioner General Picard and other high Off
cials of the Exposition arrived shortly after the
accident and superintended the work of relief
President Loubet sent officer of his house
hold for information. Several soldiers
among the injured. and many of their comrades
were foremost in giving assistance.


The disaster was the leading topic of discus
sion in the cafes and at other Paris resorts this
evening, and strong criticism levelled
against the Exposition authorities for allowing
unfinished structure to teopardize the lives
of citizens. fears being expressed that the in
complete state of the works within the Exposi-
accident. 1t should be said however that the
Exposition authorities not responsible for
the defective construction of the foot tbridge
which was erected by tn management of the
Celestial Globe

which are considered dangerous.

The swordfish is utterly without fear
and will, like buffalo or rhinoceros,
charge anything that offends it, often
doing an amount of execution hardly
to be believed did not the evidence ex-
lst, says the San Francisco Call. Com
bats between swordfish are most inter
esting and may be compared to a duel
between two expert swordsmen. Such
contest was observed off the long
pier that extends out into the ocean at
Santa Monica, near Los Angeles, last
year. Some fishermen noticed two big
fish leaping out of the water and
dashing along the surface. Soon it
was seen that they were swordfish.
The season was when the fish are un-
usually ferocious. They had made
several rushes and when observed
were at close quarters, striking each
other powerful side blows like cavalry
men. This was unsatisfactory. and
hnally they separated and darted at
each other like arrows, the water hiss
ing as their sharp dorsal fins cut
through it. They evidently struck
head on, one missing, while the sword
of the other struck just below the eye
and plowed a deep furrow in the fish,
partly disabling it, so that it turned
and attempted to escape But its ad-
versary also turned and with a rush
drove its sword completely through the
body of its foe and held it fast, only
its weapon loose when it's
enemy stopped swimming.

Taku. Aug. 80, via Shanghai. Sept. 3-The

At that time most of the population. except

are returning to their homes, only to find
shelter or rice or occupation. In the over
crowded, famine threatened districts away from
the river their lives and small possessions
at the mercy of bands of soldiers travelling
about without officers.


The conditions prevailing leave little ground
for the favorable comparison OF civilized war
fare with Chinese methods. Robbery. ravishing
and murder are so common that every respon-
sible person one meets contributes stories from
personal observation. The walled city of Tung-
Chow was the only town in the pathway Of the
international forces whose people remained and
attempted to continue business. During the
cupation the Japanese patroIled the place ef-
hciently, protected the people and prevented
looting beyond the amount inevitable with any
army. General Chaffee stationed a guard
around the historic temple outside the wall,
forbidding his troops to enter. The commanders
encouraged the inhabitants to resume bust
ness. promising protection to all peaceful per-
sons.


When the armies advanced, however, the
guards were removed, only a small British and
American garrison being left outside the wall.
A correspondent Of The Associated Press, re-
turning from Peking, found Tung- Chow stripped
like cornfield after plague OF grasshoppers.
Everything portable, of the smallest value, had
been taken-goods from shops. clothing food
and furniture. Parties Of soldiers Of every ma
tionaIity were roaming about unrestricted, and
presumably were doing much wanton destruc-
ton in the spirit of deviltry, smashing furni-
ture and glassware. and trampling books and
pictures under foot Most OF the Chinese were
submitting to all this in abJect fear. The few
who dared to protest were kicked about.


Several bodies lay in the streets. apparently
those Of on-combatants. The inhabitants
without food or clothing. were huddlng in back
yards in pitiable condition.


The villages to the southwark are even
despoiled. One week after Picking taken

sight of burning houses. Fires are started daily
although the shelter will be much needed If the
troops are to hold the country during the win
ter.

natives who creep back to their houses or at
tempt to work in the fields targets. The
sight of farmer lying where he was shot. with
a basket of grain or armful OF other produce
near by is quite common. The Russians are the
chief actors in this style of conquest, but the
French are remarkably conspicuous. considering
their small numbers. The Indian troops and the
Japanese are participants only when beyond the
ken of their officers

recital OF notorious facts speaks more forcibly

London. May 13 a. m.-General Roberts has
entered Kroonstad and completed the second
stage Of his march to Pretoria His left wing
marched twenty miles along the railway Friday
and encamped within fourteen miles of the
town. with the Beers in intrenched position at
BOschrand, six miles distant. The right wing
also advanced steadily along the Winburg road
the cavalry brigade overtaking the Boer convoy
near Nentersburg and capturing a portion of
the wagons. Pole-Carew's division was on the
extreme left, with fuckers division further east
and Cove's division on the extreme right Four
brigades of cavalry and two divisions of mount
ed infantry We're in advance OF the infantry
supports. and the bulk of the mounted force
was under French's command near the railway
A hundred prisoners had been taken, but
mishap had occurred to troop of Inniskillings
which had been suddenly fired upon from
house where the white flag was flying several
men being killed and sixteen wounded or capt
ured


The Beers evacuated their ntrenched position
al Boschrand during the night when they
learned that French's cavalry had seized drift
over the Valsch, and Pole -Carew's battalions
took possession of the trenches without opposi-
ton The following morning the British left
wing was within eight miles of Sroonstad at 9
O'clock. and the Headquarters Staff entered the
town without opposition at 1:30, followed by
the Imperial Yeomanry and other forces. The
flag was raised and cheered, and the battalions
as they came up encamped around the town
The march of 12O miles from Bloemfontein had
been made with remarkable dispatch, and Cen
eral Roberts's army had gone two-ffths of the
way to Pretoria.


General Robertss bulletin issued at o o'clock,
recited the details of the occupation of Kroon-
stad The most important detail was evidence
Of dissensions among the allies. The Transvaal
Bc=rs had refused TO remain longer in the Free
State, and had retreated across the VaaI to their
own territory. President Steyn had appealed in
vain to the burghers to make final stand, and
had himself taken refuge in flight Friday night
after proclaiming another capital in a remote
section. General Botha had gone with the
Transvaal Beers, and also General Dewet, with
a portion Of the Free Staters but apparently,
the breach between the allies final. The
Transvaal Beers would only fight in defence of
their own territory, and the mass Of the Free
staters were unwilling TO cross the Vaal. Many

the commanders with reduced numbers were

From the Youths Companion.


IT is said that the best footmates of the
Nineteenth Century were william and Mary
Hewitt. the writer's Of so many charming
bits Of literature. They began to walk on
their wedding day, and kept on walking
during nearly sixty years of married life.


In 1894. when walking was far from
fashionable, this sturdy Quaker pair
walked 500 miles among the Scotch noun
tains. carrying necessary luggage on their
strong young backs. They climbed Ben
Lomond. waded streams. crawled over
bogs, scrambled through bracken and slid
down sheer defiles In the course of this
wild tramp. Doubtless the peasants fancied
they were mad.


In the fifty-first year Of their married
life. when Mrs. Hewitt was over 70 and her
husband almost 50. they started out one
summer morning to climb an alp OF the
Tyrol From the village of Taufers they
climbed a road too steep for vehicles,
walking steadily for FIVE hours.


At dusk they came to a farmers chalet;
there they were cordially invited to sup
per, and there for two nights they slept
on the sweet. fresh hay in the barn. and
employed the days in twice climbing to the
mountain top.


An excursion which had been planned for
William Howitts birthday. sitter ne had
passed his eightieth year, was reluctantly
abandoned because of the rain. A year
or two later his wife wrote:


Father and have just come in from a
pleasant walk right into the country.
amongst picturesque houses and such
ancient orchards and parklike fields scat
tered over with grand old Spanish chest
nuts"


Mr.. Hewitt died In 1879. aged "a. For a
few years more his faithful footmate took
quiet strolls and gathered the flowers her
husband loved. And when she had lived to
see 50 years she gently fell asleep.

A dispatch from BIRMINGHAM Ala SAYS:
rainfall of almost seven inches in twen-
ty-four hours-the heaviest on record in
Alabama-has done great damage to prop
erty and caused several fatalities. Among
the victims of the storm was the Rev. o.
B. Wilson, superintendent of Stillman Insti-
tute, a Presbyterian college for the educa-
ton of colored preachers. He was struck
by lightning while at the telephone and in
stantly killed.


In Wills valley, Wills creek overfiowed its
bounds, and the house of Jacob Restler,
containing himself. his wife and five chill
dren. was carried down the creek Restler
and his wife and oldest child escaped, but
two children. aged two and four years.
were drowned. Their bodies have not been
recovered.


Village creek near Birmingham over
flowed its bounds and many negroes saved
their lives and those of their families by
swimming and improvising hasty rafts. Two
children were drowned.


The Louisville and Nashville railroad the
Alabama Great Southern, the Southern, the
Mineral and the Kansas City, Memphis and
Birmingham had numerous washouts, and
were all compelled to annul trains.


At Bangor Cave and Blount Springs the
Louisville and Nashville was five feet under
water. All trains on the Alabama Great
Southern had to make transfers of passen-
gers at several points and were from six to
eight hours late. The same state of affairs
exists other roads. Many short lines
have no trains running at all.


The water works reservoir at Bessemer
broke its bounds and submerged all the in
dustries of the lower portion of the city.
Fires were quenched in the big pipe works
and other plants. Williamson and North
Birmingham blast furnaces had to bank
fires on account of the overflow.


Dozens of coal mines in the Birmingham
district were filled with water. The mines
at Pratt City, Belle Ellen, Brookwood.
Horse Creek and numerous other places
have closed down until they can be drained.


All the suburban street car lines were
embarrassed and some suspended opera
uonS.


Reports of disaster continue to come in,
but owing to the fact that telegraph lines
are down, many points where the flood is
known to have been severest have not been
heard from. 1t will take the mines, fur
naces and mills week to resume regular
operation.


The entire town of Northport, in Tusca-
loosa county. is under water and cut of
from telegraphic communication. Several .
fatalities occurred.


. Houses and human bodies have been seen
floating down the Warrior river from
Northport.

Manila, Aug. 12-Reports from the Visayan
islands show that there has been increased ac-
tivity among the insurgents there during the
last six weeks. The American losses in the
island Of Panay last month were greater than
in any month since January last.


General Mojica, in Leyte. and General Luc-
ban in Samar. are harassing the garrisons.
shooting into the towns during the night and
ambushing small parties. firing and then re-
treating upon the larger bodies. The rebels
possess an ample supply Of ammunition and are
organized to a considerable degree. The Amer
leans have garrisoned three towns Samar
Island two of which shelter tenth of the
original inhabitants, who suffer from the con-
tinual "sniping" of the rebels from the sur
rounding hills. The third is without any native
inhabitants, the rebel outposts a mile away,
preventing their return to their homes General
Lucban Furnishes the islanders who have any
relations with the Americans Cebu is like
wise disturbed.


Barring those who have taken the oath Of
allegiance to the United States. the rebels are
imprisoned in Manila


When amnesty was proclaimed it practically
without effect, and the expectation that
the proclamation would accomplish much in
the unexpired time is daily diminishing.


The banks, under Government pressure, have
restored the exchange rate of two Mexican
silver dollars to gold American dollar. Gen
eral Macarthur has ordered the acceptance of
American money for all public dues at the
above rate.


General Wright, Major Maus and others have
returned from a trip to Benguet Province where
they recommend the immediate establishment
of a convalescent hospital. Benguet is tranquil.


The Philippine Commission, it is an

pontments.

North American Indians always treated

rock. the professor found that he had wan
dered far from his party and started in

the tin box containing bugs and insects

soon overlook him, and in sign language
ordered him to dismount


They proceeded OF once to make an in
spection Of his possessions. He had moth
ing with which to defend himself his out

to plunge their hands into his pockets,
bringing them out filed with the rock
specimens.


Again and again they did this, until pock-
cts. pouch and sadd-ebags were all emptied.
AS the pile Of stones increased upon the
ground beside him the Indians burst into
loud laughter. Finally they opened the tin
box, and when they cav nothing in that but
bugs and other insects they quickly closed
it, and. looking at one another, and then
very closely at Prof. Hayden. they touched
their foreheads and made the sign signify
ing crazy.


Then they gave back all his things even
picking up the specimens and replacing
them carefully in his pockets, pouch and
saddlebags. and in the sign language told
him to mount his horse and go on.

Mrs Harriet Maxwell Converse honorary
chief of the New York state Iroquois In
dians has left this city to attend the an
nual green corn dance at the Cattaraugus
reservation near Buffalo.


One object of Mrs Converse's visit is
TO make final arrangements with the New
York state Indians for new industry just
opening among them. This is to dig roots
and for the first time in history give the
secrets of their medicines in exchange for
money. For many years the Indians of
the western part of the state earned a good
deal of money picking fruit for the can
ming factories that fringe their reservation.
They began with the strawberries in June
ard were busy through the season until the
last tomatoes were picked. just before the
fall frosts But the Poles, who have been
swarming in great numbers into that part
of the country. and who can live on very
little, have superseded the Indians by
working for much less money.


Among the roots used by the Indians are
the wild violet the laurel sumach and
V itch hazel. They also use wild cherry
bs rk and hemlock buds. Their drugs are
compounded with the most violent poisons.


There were 1850 Indians in this state
when the last census was taken, and fully
five-eigh hths of these are pagans. says Mrs
Converse. AT their dances the people ad-
here TO the old-time superstitions and cus-
toms.

The reply satisfied the defenders of KIM

surrounding the troops and intermingling

sembled. No horse food was left.

thus kept them quiet.


The miles of convoy bearing provisions
for the relief column and the town, slowly
winding its way across the plain in the di-
rection of Kimberley, was the gladdest
sight which greeted the eyes of the be-
sieged for four months.


Gen. French's march was so rapid and
the heat was so intense that many Of his
horses died of exhaustion.

Beers bolted. leaving their tents, guns.
oxen, wagons and large quantities of am
munition in the hands of the British Nov
ing northward, the Beers again attempted
to stem the advance, but Gen. French
turned their flank and reached his goal
with Insignificant losses-seven men killed
and thirty-five wounded during three days,
from Wednesday, February IA, to Friday,
February 16. After nights rest at KIM
berley. Gen. Frenchs column pursued the
Beers to Brontveld, surrounded the copies
on which they were posted and sheiled
them till nightfall, when the Beers fled,
leaving many dead.

PUEBLO, Col, May 23.-After being
rope for 200 yards, and after the rope had

blern, murderer was lynched at 1913 o'clock

watched the death struggles and finally the

Affairs had been at fever heat in Pueblo

ments were announced from the telegraph
Office, and frequent bulletins kept every
body posted.

At 1870 o'clock last night a report was
current that the officials of the Rio Grande
railroad had issued orders to rush all trains
past the Sth street station without stop
ping. A pile Of ties twelve feet high was
quickly placed on the tracks just north of

dispatcher to notify the engineers of all
trains that they must be brought to a
standstiM and search permitted.

freight The red lanterns were swung

dozen men jumped on the engine and asked

train. They were assured that he had not.

searching every car, but the negro was not
found

allowed to proceed This was kept up until
the arrival Of the Rio Grande train at 1:15.

board at once surrounded the train at the
Sth street pot, overpowered the officers

moose was cast about his neck. Many

helpless. He was dragged face downward

ened about his neck. and he Was undoubted-

Twice the rope broke after the body had
been hauled up, but the third attempt at
hanging was successful After the body

ing. The mob then hooked the manacles

kimblern assaulted and murdered two

eminent through scorn, perhaps, for all that
suggested courts and monarchical institutions,
neglected in the early days to establish rules of
precedence for the guidance of the Nations Off
Gals which oversight is responsible for bitter
cont OVERSEES, historic feuds and innumerable
heartburns. To the President, naturally, was
accorded the first place, but the relative posi-

fixed. The Weep President sometimes took pre-
cedence of the Secretary of State, at other times
he followed humbly behind that august official,

acter of the men who held these offices For
years until indeed, the act of 1886, the wives
of the Senators insisted that the women of the
Cabinet and of the Supreme Court should make
the first call upon them, contending that, as the
members of the Cabinet and the Justices were
confirmed by the Senate, that body outranked
them.


When the English Legation was raised to the
highest rank. Sir Julian, now Lord, Pauncefote,
who was named Ambassador assumed that.
the personal representative of his sovereign, he
ranked above all the American officials the
Chief Executive. Mr. Hobart contested this as
sumption, maintaining, quite correctly, that
since, in of the Presidents death. the Vice
President would succeed him, the Vice-Presi~
dent outranked both the Ambassadors and the
Cabinet.


For months this matter in allegiance. Mr..
Hobart would not call on the English Ambassa-
dor, Lord Pauncefote declined to visit the Vice
President refused all invitations to dine where
that official was included among the guests, and
on one occasion stated quite distinctly in his re-
grets the reason for his refusal The situation be-
came finally SO embarrassing that the President
invoked the aid of the American Ambassador

Mrs White determined, in the first flush

going to be 'squeezed' by the Chinese
cook and the storekeeper, as 1t was quite
plain every one else was. Accordingly, she
purchased scales and weights, and an
nounced her intention Of personally weigh

sometimes a little puzzled on finding that
the provisions occasionally weighed more
than was charged for. One day the mys-
terry was. solved. She was, carefully weigh
ing chicken. In China, not only is every
thing, living and dead, sold by weight, but
fowls are always supplied alive. The
chicken during the weighing operation sud-
denly entered vigorous objection, and be-
gan to flap and struggle with all its might,
and during these fiappings and strugglings
something weighty fell With a thud to the
floor. evidently from somewhere about the
chicken. This turned out to be a large
piece of lead, which had been cunningly
fastened under one of the wings. Further
investigation led to the discovery of SINH
lar piece underneath the other wing. The
overweight of the past few days was now
accounted for.

Two new armored trains for employment
over country where there are no rails or
permanent ways have just been placed
upon the establishment at Aldershot, Each
consists Of locomotive or traction engine
and four trucks, all of which are painted
the now familiar. but ever unloveIy, khaki.
The locomotives, which are exceedingly
powerful construction. are completely cased
with steel. the vital parts being especially
protected. An ingenious arrangement of
prisms and mirrors, somewhat after the
manner of the camera obScura, enables the
driver inside the cab of the engine to see
without being seen, OF in any way exposing
himself The trucks are built with high
sloping steel sides. which are pierced and
slotted at intervals to enable the occupants
to fire through them. They are also pro-
vided with slides at either end to permit
of guns and wagons being run into the
trucks. The steel sides of the carriages
are so constructed that when necessary
they may fall inward and lie fiat on the
platform of the truck. which can then be
used for ordinary transport purposes.

| The ancient stone walls of the Chi
| nese city of Tien Tsin, surrounded or
| the days of its occupation by the


allied troops, square mile of such
| filth, ruin and death, such Turmoil


and pilage as history could hardly dupli-
| cate Under normal conditions the place
| was nothing better than a huge cesspoo
| fostering with the accumulated rubbish and
| Stops from a population Of nearly million
| packed into a labyrinth of novels, around
| the palaces of viceroys and petty taotais
| who absorbed their wealth and gave them
| not even sewers in return. Now 1t is the
incarnation of all the suffering, horrors and
| waste of war. The European soldiers,
| when they fought their way up to the
| walls saw floating in the canals and
bitches outside dozens Of Chinese slain by
| their own people because they refused to
| fight The bodies were headless and their
| hands were tied behind their backs. The
heads were discovered afterward. Rows OF
| them decorated the outer wallis hung by
| thei- pigtails


Five flags were flying from the high pa
| godas on the city walls when the news
paper correspondents entered, the French
Japanese, American, Russian ana bTlllSH
1T was hard enough to get those flags UP
| there" remarked foreign officer. but the
real trouble will be to get them down."
The suburbs of the city presented a
torn the huts and powed the ground while
| dead men scattered about among dead
horses. pigs and dogs testified how thor
oughly the bullets had swept the region the
day before.


Chinese Dead Everywhere.
The sights inside compelled respect for
the fighting qualities of the Chinese. Their
dead were everywhere. Dressed in the
coarse blue coolie blouse and trousers. dec
GRATED with characters guaranteed to rem
der them invulnerable to foreign bullets,
they were strewn all along the top of the
wall wherever they had fallen. Walking a
quarter of mile along the embankment,
the bodies averaged one in ten feet, and the
wall was nearly ten miles long.


Throughout the city the demolished
houses and hundreds of killed gave EVIL
dence of how vastly more effective had
been the foreign shell fire within the walls
of the city than the Chinese bombardment
of the foreign settlement. which, lasting
for month, had killed only dozen peo-
pie. The viCeroy had constructed in the
trable bomb proofs, excavations guarded
by sandbags, but the common people were
less fortunate. Many women and children
were lying dead in the streets, torn terri





utterly Indifferent to their dead. They
would not take the trouble to drag them
out of the streets or even cover them with
mating, as foreign soldier did afterward.
but trampled them under foot without
bothering to turn aside. Before the shoot
ing in the streets was finished thousands
of Chinese had emerged from their bur-
rows, carrying white flags the flags of
foreign nations, principally the Japanese


The LOOtinE of the City.





looting of the city. The middle place was
like an ant hill kicked open. Chinese
swarmed everywhere, thousands and thou
sands of them; diving into the flames of
the burning shops, getting under falling
walls and into choking clouds of smoke
Most of them were half naked. grimy with
smoke and sometimes dripping with blood.
They preyed upon one another. A Chinese
appearing with prize must fight his way.
Other Chinese sprang upon him and clutch
ed his plumber They rolled among the
corpses. pulling and tearing, while chill
dren, being trampled down, cried for help
and the mob poured right along over them


The palaces, the mint. the pawnShOps,
the stores of silks, furs and jewelry, were
the first object of attack. Near the middle
of the city was the most prosperous pawn
shop, an institution that had probably ex-
listed for centuries. Wealthy Chinese were
accustomed to store their winter clothing
there for safe keeping. When the doors
were battered down they flowed in like a
tidal wave There were British officers
naval and military soldiers and sailors,
with good sprinkling of Sikhs, but prin-
cipally Chinese. In a twinkling all was
pandemonium. The Chinese knew where
the best treasure was to be found, and the
soldiers followed them. Two forces col
lided in the gateway-a rush line Of Chi
nese struggling to enter and another line
fighting to get out with great armfuls of
loot, while an occasional soldier went
no of ha
way squad Tien Tsin experienced a sweep
ing redistribution of wealth, but on the
old scheme of prizes to the strongest.


Plundered for Three Days.


The looting f1ourished for three days. On
the first day 1t was entirely unrestrained.
Many white people accumulate d stacks of
goods by simply standing at the city
gates and holding up the best-laden Chi
nese from the endles procession that
flowed out Pack horses. carts, rickshaws.
coolies loaded with trunks and sacks filled
with loose silks, furs and bronzes. crowded
all the roads leading down to the settlement.
English officers rode with their horses con-
cealed under dry goods. and soldiers slung
bundles on their bayonets.


On the second day conference Of COM
manding officers decided to adopt repressive
measures. The commanders. excepting the
French, empowered the British. who were
doing provost duty, to seize all loot This
order the British attempted to execute by
holding up the hooters they entered the
foreign towns. They took all bundles and
reported the names of claimants for future
inquiry. Naturally this step provoked
grumblings particularly among the soldiers
Of other nationalities. Capt Bailey, the
provost marshal. a big-bodied big-voiced
Englishman. explained that the prohibition
was designed to restrain civilians from get
ting the spoils which should go to the men
who did the fighting. The officials say
that all seized loot will be sold the pro-
ceeds to be divided among the soldiers as
prize money, but soldiers. wise through
former campaigns. comment skeptically.
The Japanese. so far casual observa-
ton showed did the least looting because
of the admirable discipline under which
their soldiers are held. The Americans had
all to themselves one large arsenal, which
tanned not only cannon, but fine store of
small arms. swords of curious and rich
pattern. rifles Of various makes with stands
of the long two-man guns which are simply
giant rifles. throwing a ball which, from
| the report and whistle, the soldiers in the
| fight judged to be one-pounders. Munitions
| of war were not the only contents Of the
arsenal. High officers had lived there. and
| in flight had left stacks of clothing and
other articles of great value. All this stuff
| is to be sold or shipped to Washington as
| spells of war.


Better Plan Adopted.

more effective method was followed nv

Smythe contends that the decision holds

maintained, declared that certain sched-
ules were unreasonably low, but did

whole.

prise to railroad attorneys, who regard

the whole question of maximum freight
rates IN this state.

cruiser Variag. which left Cramps ship
yard last Tuesday for her builders trial

having been given satisfactory test. The
big warship was tried out in every con-
ceivable way, and not one weak spot was

head of steam was perfect

coast, during which time she maintained a
steady twenty-one-knot gait.

guns on the port side, four in number Were

Sir Arthur Sullivan, who died suddenly
yesterday in England. gave the world much
pleasure in his time. His music was of
character to reach the average taste. 1t
was tuneful and easily remembered. 1t
set pitch for the people of two continents
and for at least decade and half it
was the most popular of all musical COM
position. The operas which Sullivan COM
posed in collaboration with the librettist
Gilbert were wonderfully successful. For
several years product from these two men
was assured in advance of an enthusiastic
reception. "Pinafore" became almost an
institution. The bright lines and the grace
full airs of that opera caDtivated all hear
ers and when it was followed by such
other successes as the Pirates Of PEN
zance." Patience" The Mkado' and The
Gondoliers, together with several other
less successful operas, 1t was evident that
the two amusement furnishers had estab


lished a record not likely soon to be broken.
Sullivan wrote other and more ambitious
music than these operas. and his influence
some. Few men leave such enduring mem
cries behind them. The world will be
whistlng airs from Sullivan's compositions
probably generations hence when more
serious operate efforts have been entirely
relegated to the musical pigeon hole.

gan. There were forty-fve guns In all In the

A7-inch and the Japanese s-centimetre Krupp

with few Austrian marines. They unlimbered

Washington Oct. 27-The work of counting

and next week Director Merriam will announce
the population of the country. His statement.
however, will be subject to some slight revision.
All the returns from Alaska are not yet IN, and
the returns from the American soldiers and
sailors serving in the Philippines ard elsewhere
abroad not complete. These figures will be
estimated. The figures for the States and Ter
ritories will be official


The work Of the present census has proceeded
i system entirely different from that of the
last census The first count of the population
under the last census a hand count, and
was completed on Thanksgiving Day, 1890 The
work of punching the individual cards contain
ing individual statistics was not begun until
March, 1891 and was not completed until Sep
TENDER, 1891 The present count has proceeded
as each card has been punched, that now,
with the completion of the count the individual
statistics punched in the cards complete.


The other statistics be ground out
mechanically from the punched cards. After
the total population and the population bY
States and Territories are announced next week,
the bulletin showing the population of the States
and Territories by minor civil divisions Will be
issued soon as tabulated.

Charleston. s. C., August 22.-(SpecialD
The unprecedented heat wave which has
been hanging over this immediate section
for the past ten days or more, has play
ed deadly havoc with the poor negroes
living on the sea islands along the coast.
From the best accounts received here it
appears that the negroes have been dying
from fever. which IS primarily caused
from the heat and allowed TO thrive be
cause the sick cannot get the medical at
teEtion required in such cases. During
the summer season the island negroes
live on almost anything they can get TO
eat and this puts their systems in fine
tim for disease.


Undertaken Livingston. of Charleston.
wEo takes care Of tho island negroes after
they are dead. said today that he was
hardly able TO stand the calls which had
been made on him for cheap collins. He
rrade the bald statement that the island
negroes are dying like sheep and that
when they become I'll OF the fever they
simply have TO walt their turn to Gle
The sea islands are densely populated
with negroes and in the low swamps
where malaria thrives, the negroes. who
are no more than paupers in time of sick
ness. are left to suffer the fierce heat
through the days and nights of the agon-
izirg fever. and the crisis is generally
passed with death.


In some of the sections the voodoo doc
tcrs have been making more victims Tor
the undcrtakers. These are the witch
people. and there are hundreds of them
on the islands, who believe that a little
magic is all-sufiicicnt to heal disease.
These alleged doctors are a great deal
worse than the Christian science freaks
and their work for negroes near Charles
tor. has brought tOrth deadly peril.


This summer there has been more fever
on the sea Stands than for some years
past and this disease has been sent thriv-
ing on by the hot and dry weather. PeO-
pie who have been around sick rooms
with fever patients can best imagine the
condition of the poor negroes in the hoy
els who have TO depend on voOdOoism for
relief ana who have 10 stay in a serious
way without proper attention and with
Out Ice. The island negroes have felt
the bitterness of II all, and they simply
lie down and die when the fever strikes
them. In some of the huts il has been
told here that "A whole family would be i'll
at time and that their only attention
would come from the neighbors who were
inclined to lend assistance.


The physicians in these island nelghbor-
hoods have done their best TO give relief
to the negroes and pretty much all of
this has been charity. Even with charity
physicians, how ever the sufferers have
not been cared for as their condition
might demand. and with weird shouting
and chanting about them they have laid
down to die, with nothing more than a
voodoo doctor to drive off the ills.


The class OF negroes now suffering from
the diseases brought on by the heat are
the ones who suffered most a few years
ago by the terrible storms which swept
up the coast. Families were drowned and
there was great agony for those who
escaped. Another trouble with which
these sick negroes have had TO deal IS
the pest of mosquitoes and sandfiies
which Will drive sane man mad. The
sting of these pests adds terror to the
negroes. but II helps to make the stiIfg
OF death more welcome. and the blacks
have doubtless found great relief IN
death.

BALTIMORE. Md, March 21-Like one
returning from the dead the Spanish steam
ship Minerva steamed into port this after
noon, after having long ago been given up
for lost with all on beard. She was storm
beaten and rusty, and her crew were
hungry looking and exhausted. and when
she anchored in Canton hollow all on board
breathed sigh of relief.


January II she sailed from Porman,
Spain, for Baltimore with a cargo of iron
ore. which trip she should have made in
sixteen days.


She encountered terrific weather and her
coal gave out. February 81 she was sighted
by a British steamship, helpless in terrific
gale, and an effort was made to tow her
This failed and the steamer left her. Moth
ing more was heard from her for weeks,
and the United States revenue steamer
Onondaga made three trips, far out to sea
to seek her. but failed to find her. She
was given up for lost and her insurance
paid. Her captains wife in Bilboa Spain,
went in mourning for him, as Gid the rela-
tives of her officers and crew, but this
morning she turned up safe and sound She
was picked uo about ten days ago and
towed into Bermuda, where she coaled and
proceeded.

rear driver and jolting the train terrihcally.

the train seemed TO have left the tracks. Hines
and the fireman stuck to their posts and put the
air brakes and the big engine, after ploughing
along the tracks for three hundred yards,
brought to a standstill. The passengers rushed
Of the cars and went forward to find side OF
the engine wreck and Hines coolly gazing at the
damage done. Hines applauded and congratu-
lated by the passengers when they learned the risk

London, Jan. 13-Though many stirring scenes
have marked the departure OF the British troops
FOR the front during recent months to-day's
outburst of patriotism on the occasion of the
starting of the London Volunteers was unprece-
dented since the Jubilee It is the first time in
the history of the movement that British volun-
teers have been permitted to serve side by side
with the regulars in real warfare, and the peo-
pie turned out in hundreds of thousands fit
ungly to celebrate it. The crowds began to
throng the route before dawn and increased in
such proportions that a detachment of the Lord
Mayors Own engufed at various stages
Of the march. The ranks were broken and the
troops at times were almost lost sight of in the
cheering, shouting, singing mob. Every now
and then halt had to be made in order to re-
form the ranks, but only to be again broken,
the police were utterly unable to stem the
cited mass of people. The handshakings and
embracings were so exuberant that the original
smartness of the volunteers was speedily i'm
paired many uniforms being torn. But the
troops finally managed to struggle through to
the Mansion House On the balcony of that
building the Lord Mayor, A J. Newton; the
Lady Mayoress the Councillors and others
awaited the arrival of the volunteers and wit
messed them actually fighting their way through
the dense crowds. assisted by male friends and
impeded by clinging women When the force
was finally reformed the Lord Mayor attempted
to make speech but found II impossible. The
din was simply deafening. and the Chief Magis-
trate had to be content to indicate his good
wishes by smiles and gestures while the volun-
teers greeted him with cheers and waving of
hats their raised rifles.


There was another herculean effort on the
part of the police, and the detachment resumed
its march, to the accompaniment of pushing
screaming cheering and singing The column
had hardly covered hundred yards when it
again 'ntermingled with the surging crowds,
who had undisputed sway along the route
Many Of the volunteers escaped through side
streets and others struggled along in Indian
file twos or threes. BY the time they reached
the Thames Embankment the detachment had
become a conglomeraton, wOmen's hats being
as numerous n the ranks the volunteers
headgear. So slow was the progress that over
an hour was consumed in traversing the mile to
Westminster. There the police arrangements
improved and the multitudes were marshalled
into some kind of order. The windows roofs
and every other vantage point were crowded
with singing and cheering humanity waving
banners, hats and handkerchiefs.


Finally, the column reached Nine Elms Sta
ton, bearing numberless traces of the difficult
ties of the march. The public was excluded
the final leavetakings being held outside, and
the volunteers entrained and departed amid
commingling Of band music and cheering and
the singing of "Auld Lang Syne" Rule Britain
MIA" and God Save the Queen"


The Lord Mayor Sheriffs and Councillors, IN
their State robes, accompanied by many women
took another special train for Southampton 10
bid farewell to the volunteers on board the
transport Briton. The volunteers arrived soon
after the Lord Mayors party, and were saluted
with ringing cheers from huge assemblage on
the quays as they boarded the liner.


Immense crowds filled the streets OF South
ampton as the volunteers boarded the transports
Briton and Garth Castle. Many of the soldiers
carried Union Jacks their guns, while in
several instances these were supplemented by
the Stars and Stripes, which evoked great en-
thusiasm from the crowds.


The Lord Mayor the Lady Mayoress and
many officials took luncheon on board the trans
ports, which finally sailed amid the footing of
whistles the cheers of the crowds, and the
playing of national anthems by the bands


About four thousand troops sailed for South
Africa this afternoon.
