The ''multum in parvo" furniture, among
which are the wardrobe couch, the writing desk
dressing case and various other composite ar
rangements, is regarded by most people
essentially the result of modern ingenuity.
In point of fact, hardly a single instance
of the kind lacks It's prototype dating from
medieval times when life was too nearly
a from day to day" affair to permit
many household gods to accumulate. No
one knew, not even the powerful, when
he might be obliged to flee from maraud
ing neighbors, and the furniture consisted prin-
cipally of large chests for plate, linen and vest
ures. These were called standards in England,
and served as seats and tables by day and beds
at night, They were Of immense size. and as
luxury increased were richly carved and orna-
mented with wrought iron.


AS social conditions improved and habitations
became less uncertain, the armory and other
pieces came into use. The armory was the pred
ecessor of the sideboard, and was used for
safekeeping of valuables being made Of heavy
wood, reinforced by wrought iron. 1t at
first little more than handsome chest stood on
end. The armory found a supplement in the
cupboard-a structure of uninclosed shelves for
the display of silver and other treasures. Then
the cupboard and armory were combined. and
the result called a credence, It had both
shelVes ana locked compartments.


After a time these carved and decorated
credences became the subject OF restrictions
that to-day seem most tyrannical and absurd.
The queen might have as many shelves as she
wished, and could cover them with cloth of gold,
but countess could have no more than three,
and knights lady only the original form, a
chest on legs The back might be carved or
covered with silk, and damask napkins covered
the shelves. that served the purpose of the
cabinet now In use, and held all kinds Of curious
and beautiful articles Frequently the credence.
or court cupboard, as II came to be called had
a canopy of wood.


The buffet for carving and for extra dishes and
silver variation of the credence.


The chest that served as seat bed and table
was divided in time into its component parts.
The first table board trestles, while
the chest remained a seat. Gradually the table
became stationary in construction and varied
in design. Sometimes 1t was round, sometimes
shaped like horseshoe or semi-circle, the guests
sitting around the outside and being served
from within. Cloths were used early as the
thirteenth century, and little later came sur
napes" of damask. embroidered and fringed, for
use when the basins of rosewater were carried
around the table. These were the ancestors of
the table napkin.


The seats were bancs-whence the term BAN
Quet-hnally benches, often with iacks and
arms The chair reserved for the lord Of
the castle until much later period.


The bed of the twelfth century plat
form -ornamented legs Then the supports
were extended above the platform, and finally
heightened to receive a canopy. In the thir-
teenth century the bed was rallied about with
gateway at one side and low step. Some
of these beds were twelve feet wide. and there
slept parents children and dogs. The hangings
were superb-silk and golden tapestry-so that
they were valuable bequests


Curtained wardrobes appeared to protect rich
robes. and soon doors were added. These were
handsomely carved, enamelled and painted or
otherwise decorated


The sofa is merely an evolution from the bench
to which back and ends were added as protec-
tion from draughts. 1t at first compro-
mise between the thrOnelike chairs which sat
the lord and lady of the castle and the long
bench which were seated all the retainers,
the shorter benches being for the honored
guests. These were covered frequently with
tapestries velvet, by way of distinction as
we'll as added comfort.

Against the Turnpike Company the
Circuit Court for Baltimore city a few days ago
Judge Sharp delivered an opinion dismissing
the suit of the Baltimore and Frederick Turn.
pike Company for an injunction restraining
the United Railways and Electric Company
from running express cars over the turnpike
between Baltimore and Gainesville and Ellicott
City.


The decision of the case turned upon the
construction of contracts entered into between
the turnpike company and the former Baiti-
more and Gainesville Railway Company
There were three of these contracts. By the
last one, executed in 1889, the railway COM
pany was given the right to carry over the
turnpike such articles as are carried on other
suburban electric lines entering the city.


The turnpike company claimed that the con-
tract is being violated by the cars of Gathers
Express, which carry articles not contemplated
by the contract. Thereby, the turnpike COM
pany alleged, it is losing large amount in the
tolls formerly paid for the wagons carrying the
goods now transported in the cars.


Judge Sharp decided that the evidence did
not show that the contract has been violated.
The Court held that the cars may carry light
freight, but not heavy freight Light freight
needed by suburban residents and storekeepers
including farmers and cottagers' supplies, fur
niture, store goods, baggage, brick and lumber
in small lots. Heavy freight was construed to
mean carload lots or larger quantities of coal,
ore, hay, produce, grain, lumber, sand, gravel
and similar articles.

Tsin.-One disadvantage that the Ameri-
| cans had during the hard march to the


relief Of Pekin that their transporta-


ton wagons were late in arriving. The 9th


Infantry possessed the only outfit which


reached Tien Tsin up to the time Of start


ing. The supplies were divided among the


soldiers of the 9th and the 14th Infantry


regiments and the battery. The Ameri-


cans, with haversacks blankets and tent


rolls, started under the heaviest loads. but
| they soon stripped to fighting trim, prefer
| ring to forego their blankets rather than
| to sweat under them. During the last two
| nights of the march they slept tired and
| worn out in the rain without shelter or
| cover.


One night the wagon train lost the road
| and passed the American camp. The


drivers plodded along four miles in the
| darkness and rain. They might have
| driven into the Chinese camp, but, fortu-


nately, the Russians stopped them just In
| time.


Went without RatiOns.
| The Americans often bivouacked supper
| less and breakfastless, and toward the end
| the officers kept the men at work only by
appealing to their national pride.


Don't let the Britishers beat you. Don't
| let the Russians get ahead" they urged
constantly.


The army transport when it reached
| Pekin was q unique spectacle. Miles of
animals, vehicles and coolies trailed behind
everything imaginable on wheels, from
farm wagons to fashionable equipages.
The Japanese had cows bearing packs,
and the Russians had camels. Cinnamon
pulled the carts, staggered under heavy
packs, the soldiers cursing and beating
them. Several dropped dead. Two hundred
junks and scOws bearing munitions were
towed up the river by coolies. Had the
Chinese taken the offensive most of the
transportation might easily have been cap
tured and cut to pieces by small thanking
parties.


After 1t waG apparent that the enemy
was demoralized the generals trusted the
transport to luck, and bent their efforts to-
ward getting ahead. Only such an emer
gency as existed could have justified such
hardships as were imposed upon the troops.


Medal for the Survivors.
A medal will be struck commemorating
the siege of Pekin. 1t will bear the legend:
Men, not walls, make a city,
In the grounds of the British legation,
| where a handful of men withstood the
millions of the Chinese capital for fifty
six days, a memorable celebration is in
progress tonight in vindcation of that
principle. Missionaries assembled about



Rockets are blazing. Soldiers and civilians

women are applauding the sound of can
non that smashing the yellow roofs

The tired Sikhs are planting their tents
On the lawn. and the American and Rus
sian contingents are lighting campfres

Through the ruins of the foreign settle
ment eager cosmopolitan crowd is

dies diplomats. Americans from the Phil

Saigon who Kept discreetly to the rear
while the fighting was in progress, but
came conspicuously to the front when
looting began Only the Japanese, who
have earned the first place, are absent


Luxury of Peace.


Resident foreigners welcome the luxury
of walking about and immunity from bull
let's The newcomers are anxious to in
spect the evidences of historic defense.
These barricades are, after all, the most
wonderful sight in Pekin. The barriers
hedging the British legation are mar
vel of stone and brick walls and earth
works. Sandbags shield every foot Of
space The tops of the walls have inches
for the riflemen and the buildings at their
porticoes and windows have armor boxes,
bags stuffed with dirt and pillows, too.


Back of the United States legation is a





rines held. completely screening both sides
of the walls, with steps leading to 1t.
There is a loopholed barrier across the
wall, which faces a similar Chinese work
a few yards away. Another wall bars Le-
CATION street in front of the German le-
cation, and confronting the enemys bar
ricades within those limits are yet more
walls enabling the foreigners to contract
the area Of defense If pressed.


The tops of the American and British
buildings were badly torn by the Chinese
shells The rest of the foreign settle
sand eight hundred shells fell there dur
ing the first three weeks of the lombard
ment 400 in one day. Bucketsful of bull

Four hundred and fourteen people lived
in the compound through the greater part
Of the siege. Three hundred and four ma
rines, assisted by eiehty-fve volunteers,
commanded by the English Capt. Poole.
defended the place. Eleven civilians were
killed and nineteen wounded. Fifty-four
marines and sailors were killed and 112
wounded.


Losses of the Americans.


The American loss was seven killed and
eleven wounded. Mr.. Gilbert Reid, who was
wounded in the feet. was the only American
civilian injured. Two foreign ladies were
wounded.


The reception which the survivors gave
the army was worth the hardships the

which had been the salvation of the be-

lines blocked up and telegraph and tele-

cation in all parts. There have been a
great number of accidents due to falling
chimneys and roof states, and from similar

pedestrians have sustained fractured limbs

The Florida waters are strikingly rich in
fish life, and the United States fish COM
mission has just published a check list in
small compass. which will be interesting to
anglers everywhere.


Sixteen different kinds of sharks have
been taken and identified. Among them
are the curious nurse shark. the great
tiger shark, the swift and ravenous mack
erel shark. the ugly and strange angel
shark and the huge hammerhead.


There are thirteen varieties of rays in
Guiding everything from the common barn
door skate to the electric ray and the i'm
mense butterfly ray. There are no fewer
than six varieties of the terrible sting ray,
locally known as stingarees and feared as
being fatally yenomous Strange rays are
the eagle rays, and stranger still are the
monstrous devilfish. more popularity known
as seadevils. thus being distinguished from
the octopus and the squid, which are called
deVllfiSh all over the world.


There are three varieties of garfish, the
lons-nosed garpike. the short-nosed gar and
the alligator gar, which is feared by fisher
men as much or more than shark.


Eleven species of catfish are listed, rang
Ing from the blue cat of 100 pounds and
more to the tiny fellows of one-quarter of
a pound.


Twenty-three kinds of eels are to be
found in the inland and oceanic waters of
FLORIDA There are three varieties of fierce
and serpent-like morays. There are two
varieties of tarpon, and twenty-five varie-
ties of the rest of the herring family.


Among the more curious fishes that are
not known generally are the lizard fish. the
viper fish, the snake eels. the needle and
the hound fish, the trumpet and the cornet
fish. pipe fish and sea horses, there being
four varieties of the latter: the savage var
racudas, the cutlass fishes. sawfish, amper
Jacks. moon fish. the triple tails, the rudder
fish. croakers, parrot fish. lady fish. angel
fish, trigger. file and trunk fish, buffers, or
blow fish. of which there are twelve varie
ties; the shark suckers and other remora
fishes which have fat disc like the sole
of a rubber shoe top of their heads, with
which they attach themselves by suction
to a shark or anything else; the star gaZ-
ers, which have eyes that are turned up
ward at so sharp an angle that they have
a ludicrously sanctfmonious aspect: the
hideous bat fishes, which look as if they
had escaped from the inferno; and, for
beauty, the lovely little bride fish, also
known as the foureye fish, because IT has
a deep velvety black spot just behind the
tail which looks like glowing eye.

text:
NEW YORK, February 19.-The con-
tinued cold weather following the snow
storm of Saturday and yesterday caused
but little delay in the general resumption OF
business. All the trains were running as
usual, but the ice in the rivers caused some
delay to ferry boats and shipping. The ice
filled the slips and docks and made land
ing rather difficult.


The mails resumed their wonted regu-
larity. The street cleaning department had
cleared much of the snow from the lower
portion of the city and big gang was put
to work this morning in the uptown dis
tricts. Doubly as much work, as expressed
in actual loads of snow removed in New
York, was done during the twenty-four
hours beginning yesterday morning at
o'clock as was ever done before in the
first twentyfour hours after snowfall.
Only a few loads short of an even $4,000
were removed. Something like $500 carts
were hired, besides the ones used by the
department. Over 1900 men were employed
as shovelers during the day, and an aver
age of $50 men during the two night shifts.
The men are worked in eight-hour shifts
and get 50 for the eight hours work.


The outdoor poor department of the city
charities department was besieged by poor
people today for assistance. This was par
ticularly true of the fuel supply depart
ment and the dispensary.

Special Dispatch to The Evening Star.


FREDERICK, Nd. February 19-Daniel
Smith, seventy years old, was arrested last
night at his home at Wolfsville. this
county. charged with numbering his wife
by administering poison in some pudding
which she had for supper on Wednesday
evening last. Mrs. Smith, after eating sup
per, went to the home of her daughter.
Mrs. Case, who lives near her, to help nurse
one of her children who was sick Shortly
after she arrived she was taken ill and
vomited frequently. She tlied about 3
o'clock Thursday morning in great agony.


DIR. Lamar, who was present, could not
diagnose the case and could not tell the
cause of death. Much comment was caused
in the community, and suspicion fell upon
Smith, and finally became so strong that
he was arrested and lodged in jail in Fred
erick. States Attorney Worthington, in
company with the prisoner and coroner,
will visit the house where Mrs Smith died,
and take testimony before having the body
exhumed.


Smith was seen at the Jail this morning.
and protested his innocence with tears
streaming down his wrinkled face. Smith
was tried in the Frederick county court for
the murder of man named Osborne about
twenty years ago. He is a brother of Fred
erick Smith. who was hung in Hagerstown
about thirty years ago for the murder Of
Miss Agnes Tracy, who refused to marry
him.

From yonder belfry, old and gray,


Where thick the frosted ivy climbs,
Now sweet and slow. now blithely gay,
Along the shining, wintry way,
There comes the sound of Christmas chimes;
Across the sunlit SHOWS that lie,
A glittering fleece of jewels rare,


Now grandly rising far on high,
Now borne in tenderest whispers nigh,
They fill with joy the morning air.
In tranquil calm the landscape smiles;
The spirit of all peace is here;
The simple life no passion wiles.


Nor storm, nor stress the heart peguiles
From paths by duty rendered dear,


When flashed DER Judah's plains the light
Whose luster with the ages swell;


The joy, that sweetly solemn night,
Revealed to man on Bethlehem's height,
Seems echoed here in Christmas bells.
Warmed by the yule-log's cherry blaze.


With friends around the hearth-stones wide,
In simple sports, or old-time lays,


Or legends quaint of other days,
The village keeps its Christmas tide;


Or, seated round the ample board,
Exponent true of prosperous times,


From hearts with life's contentment stored,
In homely phrase, are praises poured


That blend, perchance. with Christmas chimes
Within the manor's stately hall


Kind hearts with Christmas cheer keep pace,
And childrenS merry voices call,


And bounfeous gifts for one and all
From loving hands the season grace.


With rich or poor, with old or young,
Within each heart some memory dwells
OF bliss the by-gOne years may hold
Which now. like some sweet tale retold,
Come back again with Christmas bells.
Sweet Christmas bells, through every land
Ring out your message. far and wide;
That faith, by Love Divine. be famed.
And Gods sweet peace with men may stand,

attacked by rebels. Twenty of the Americans
were killed The remainder rescued from
annihilation.

fell upon those inside the edfce. The walls
manned intact, however. and were used
shelter by the beseged Americans for three days

sides at once.

dows and doors of the church. and did great
execution among the Filipinos. 1t is estimated
that over two hundred of the latter were killed
many dead bodies being removed from the
scene of the fighting.

a lieutenant and eight men arrived from LaOan
and engaged the besiegers, who thereupon re-
tired. The fortunate arrival of these reinforce
ments prevented the annihation of the Ameri-
force intrenched in the church who had re-
peatedly declined to surrender when ordered to
do so by the Filipinos The ten survivors were
without food. had little ammunition, and were
physically exhausted when relieved.

are acting in aggressive manner and
threatening that section of the coast particu-
larly the town of Catarma, whence the garrison
will probably be withdrawn to Laoan.

Company, Of Seattle.

Cebu. She returned here In ballast. having
had an uneventful voyage.


She began coaling tonight and will leave
tomorrow night for Seattle to load a cargo
of mules and feed for Manila. Her owners
expect she will sail in about week.

At Kansas City last night Alexander Jes-
ter. charged with the murder, twenty-nine
years ago, of Gilbert Gates, was acquitted.
When the jury filed in the court room was
filled with an expectant throng. As soon
as the jurymen were seated Judge Erby.
who was in waiting. asked Foreman Joseph
Barry If a conclusion had been reached.
Barry answered quietly in the affirmative,
and handed the written verdict to the
judge. The latter scanned 1t a moment and
then read:


I'VE, the jury, find the defendant, Alex
ander Jester, not guilty"


Jester. bent with age and worn with
watching, sat as if dazed Finally, realizing
the import of the words, the old man arose.
his face beaming with joy. He moved slow
ly toward the jurymen to thank them.


A moment later the spectators gave vent
to their feelings in a shout that made the
court room ring. With common impulse a
rush was made for the man who made so
brave fight for his life. Jester was almost
smothered with ngratulations.


After nearly four weeks of tedious testt-
mony the great trial passed into history
with the buffalo calf and Hulen Lane, and
the old man, after a second attempt to SEM
him to the gallows. had been set free. Il
had been a trial filled with pathos-pre
senting the spectacle of woman testifying
against her brother in an attempt to fasten
a crime committed nearly thirty years ago
upon his head.


There were three ballots taken In the
jury room. The first stood nine for acquittal
and three for murder in the first degree.
The next stood ten for acquittal and two
for conviction. The third and last was unan-
imous for acquittal.


As soon as Jester could tear himself away
from those who crowded about he hurried
to his hotel and was soon the center of a
happy group of his children-Harvey Jester,
Will and Alice HILL who quietly rejoiced.
Jester will leave here at once for his home
in Oklahoma, where he was arrested two
years ago.


Last night when the verdict was made
known it caused general rejoicing through
the town.
